analysis.one_liner: Directs EPA to set water pollution limits for PFAS "forever chemicals" and funds treatment plant upgrades.
analysis.headline: With 34 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote and died in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are long-lasting man-made chemicals used in nonstick cookware, waterproof clothing, firefighting foam, and many industrial processes; they do not break down and have been linked to health harms. This bill would have required the EPA to set, on a deadline, the legal limits for how much PFAS industries may discharge into rivers, lakes, and sewers, and to publish health-based water quality criteria for each measurable PFAS chemical and class [S2] [S3]. It also authorized $200 million a year from 2022 through 2026 in grants to publicly owned sewage treatment plants to help them remove PFAS from wastewater [S3]. The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Water Resources subcommittee on June 1, 2021, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water from supplies contaminated by industrial PFAS discharge, and residents of communities downstream of PFAS-emitting factories. Municipal sewage treatment plants would also gain, receiving federal grants to upgrade equipment needed to remove PFAS from wastewater [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of PFAS-contaminated communities and municipal treatment plants

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA to publish, within two years of enactment, human health water quality criteria for each measurable PFAS substance and class — the science-based thresholds for how much PFAS in water is likely to harm health [S3].

Requires EPA, within four years, to issue effluent limitations guidelines — legally enforceable discharge limits under the Clean Water Act — for nine priority industries, including organic chemicals and plastics, pulp and paper, textile mills, electroplating, metal finishing, leather tanning, paint, electronics, and plastics molding [S3].

Authorizes $200 million annually for fiscal years 2022 through 2026 in grants to publicly owned treatment works to implement the new PFAS discharge standards, shifting part of the cleanup cost from local ratepayers and municipal budgets to the federal government [S3].
Sets deadlines, addressing the pattern of EPA voluntarily taking years or decades to write effluent guidelines for PFAS; the bill made the standards mandatory with fixed publication dates [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Industries that discharge PFAS into water — chemical and plastics makers, pulp and paper mills, textile mills, electroplating and metal finishers, tanneries, paint formulators, and electronics manufacturers — would bear the cost of measuring, treating, or eliminating PFAS in their wastewater, costs that could be passed to consumers in product prices. Taxpayers would fund the $200 million-per-year grant program.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for the nine covered industries could be substantial — retrofitting wastewater treatment for PFAS is technically difficult — and some of those costs would likely be passed through to consumers in the form of higher prices for paper, textiles, electronics, and other goods [S2] [S3].

The $200 million annual grant authorization covers only a share of the upgrade bill facing thousands of publicly owned treatment works nationwide, leaving municipalities and their ratepayers to cover the rest even as they receive industrial PFAS they cannot fully remove [S3].

Fixed statutory deadlines for EPA rulemaking leave little room for the agency's usual engineering and economic feasibility analysis per industry, which critics of mandated deadlines argue can produce standards that are harder for some facilities to meet on schedule [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have imposed real, quantifiable costs on a defined set of PFAS-discharging industries in exchange for enforceable deadlines on limits of a chemical class that persists in drinking water sources and accumulates in people's bodies. The federal grants would have softened the burden on municipal utilities and their ratepayers. The main design tension is between rigid statutory deadlines and the technical difficulty of PFAS treatment, not between public benefit and private gain. On the merits, the health protections were broad and the costs fell mostly on the parties creating the pollution.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Water Resources and Environment subcommittee, which never held a markup or vote on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Pappas (D-NH) introduced the bill on May 28, 2021, joined by 30 original cosponsors, and 34 members total cosponsored it — 32 Democrats and 2 Republicans [S3] [S4].

The House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure received the bill on the day of introduction and referred it to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment on June 1, 2021; the action history shows no hearing, subcommittee vote, full committee markup, or floor action at any point afterward [S5].
The committee's chairman, Rep. Peter DeFazio (D-OR), was himself an original cosponsor of the bill, but no markup was ever scheduled under his chairmanship before the Congress expired [S3] [S5].

Because the bill never advanced past committee referral, EPA faced no statutory deadline from this bill to publish PFAS water quality criteria or industry effluent guidelines, and no federal grant program for treatment works was created by it [S3] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industries that discharge PFAS into the nation's waters — chemical, plastics, pulp and paper, textile, metal finishing, and electronics operations — avoided the mandated discharge limits and treatment costs the bill would have set, and the public continued to bear PFAS exposure without enforceable deadlines or federal treatment plant funding from this measure.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had genuine bipartisan backing at introduction — 34 cosponsors split 32 Democrats and 2 Republicans — and no recorded floor opposition, because it never reached a vote.

industries.industry: PFAS manufacturers and PFAS-using chemical producers
industries.note: The bill would have required enforceable discharge limits for organic chemicals, plastics, and synthetic fibers operations, the source category where many PFAS compounds originate, including discharges sent to public sewage plants. Their discharge cost is the public's water contamination.

industries.industry: Pulp, paper, textile, tanning, electroplating, metal finishing, paint, and electronics manufacturers
industries.note: These seven named industries would have faced effluent limitations guidelines for PFAS discharge within four years, requiring monitoring and treatment investments. The chemicals end up in water supplies those same communities drink from.

The bill authorized $200 million a year for five years in federal grants to help these plants implement the new PFAS standards, reducing the burden on local ratepayers. Their interest runs alongside residents' interest in cleaner water.
